title: Wood stamp decoration on clay
subtitle: Cutting a wooden stamp and pressing a repeating pattern into fresh clay
excerpt: A wood stamp cut from soft wood or an offcut is one of the most controlled ways to apply a repeating pattern to fresh clay. Unlike found-object textures, a cut stamp is consistent: the same impression every time, as deep and as clear as you choose. This tutorial covers cutting the stamp from softwood and using it to decorate fresh clay slabs and hand-built forms.
sourceNotes: Clay-stamping technique derived from traditional ceramic decoration practice. Wooden stamp-cutting for pottery documented across multiple ceramic traditions; technique references derived from traditional hand-building methodology.

glossaryTerms.definition: Unfired clay in any stage of drying. Stamps should be pressed while the clay is still fresh greenware.

content.text: A pottery stamp gives a clean, repeatable impression in fresh clay. Use stamps for borders, allover patterns, maker's marks, or single motifs. Commercial stamps come in bisque-fired clay or hardwood. The most satisfying ones are cut from softwood: balsa, basswood, or pine. Use a lino-cutting tool or craft knife to cut the design.

. A wood stamp: either a commercial pottery stamp or a piece of softwood with a design cut into one face using a lino-cutting tool. The design must be in relief (the raised parts create the impression in the clay), not recessed. Cornflour or talc to dust the stamp to prevent sticking.

Cut a square of soft balsa or basswood about 4 × 4 cm and 10 mm thick. Draw the design on the flat face in pencil. Keep it simple: geometric shapes (diamonds, zigzags, concentric squares), single lines, or a leaf outline.

Cut away the background wood with a lino-cutting V-tool or a craft knife, leaving the design in relief (standing proud of the cut-back background). The raised areas are what will press into the clay. Remove material in thin passes to avoid splitting the wood.

Test the stamp on a scrap of fresh clay before using it on the final piece. Dust the stamp face lightly with cornflour, press firmly straight down, and lift straight up. Check that all raised areas of the stamp made contact and that the impression is clean.
Roll the clay to the required thickness for the piece: a minimum of 6 mm so the stamp does not push all the way through. The clay should be fresh; the surface slightly damp rather than dry.
Dust the stamp face lightly with cornflour to prevent sticking. Too much cornflour blurs the impression: a very thin dusting on the raised surfaces only.

Press the stamp straight down onto the clay, applying firm even pressure across the full face of the stamp. Rock it very slightly if needed for contact on all raised areas, but keep rocking to a minimum: excessive rocking blurs the impression.

Lift the stamp straight up. Examine the impression: the design should be uniformly deep across its full area. If any section did not impress fully, re-position the stamp and press again on that area only.

A pottery stamp gives a clean, repeatable impression in fresh clay. Use stamps for borders, allover patterns, maker's marks, or single motifs. Commercial stamps are available in bisque-fired clay or carved hardwood. The most satisfying ones are cut from softwood such as balsa, basswood, or pine, using a lino-cutting tool or craft knife.
Stamp sticks to the clay: not enough cornflour, or clay too wet. Dust the stamp and let the clay surface dry for a minute before pressing.
Impression blurry: stamp rocked too much during pressing; or clay too wet. Keep the stamp square to the surface and minimise rocking.
Some parts of the design not impressing: stamp face not flat; clay slab not evenly rolled. Sand the stamp face flat, and roll the slab between level guide rails.

rows.problem: Impression depth varies across the same stamp
rows.cause: Uneven pressure during pressing; design elements at different heights on the stamp
rows.fix: Use the rolling pin to roll over the back of the stamp once it is positioned on the clay, applying even pressure across the full face.

rows.problem: Stamp splits along the grain during carving
rows.cause: Grain running across the cut direction; too deep a cut in one pass
rows.fix: Cut parallel to the grain where possible. Take multiple shallow passes instead of one deep cut.
